passages.title: The plastic problem on a small island
passages.text:
[A] The fictional island of Morra has a population of only six thousand, yet every year its beaches collect several tonnes of plastic waste. Very little of this rubbish comes from the island itself. Most of it is carried by ocean currents from countries hundreds of kilometres away, and it arrives in the largest quantities after winter storms.

[B] For years, the islanders relied on volunteers who walked the beaches with bags after each storm. The volunteers collected huge amounts, but the waste was then shipped to the mainland for disposal, which was expensive and produced its own emissions. In 2019, the island council decided that a different approach was needed.

[C] The council’s first step was to measure the problem accurately. Volunteers began sorting what they collected and recording each type of item. The results were surprising: fishing equipment, especially nets and ropes, made up nearly half of the plastic by weight, while drinks bottles, which most people had expected to dominate, accounted for less than a tenth.

[D] These figures changed the island’s strategy. Instead of focusing only on cleaning beaches, Morra began working with fishing organisations in neighbouring countries to encourage the return of old nets. A small workshop on the island now turns collected rope into mats and baskets, which are sold to tourists. The workshop employs four people and covers about a third of its costs through sales.

[E] The islanders accept that they cannot solve a global problem alone. Their records, however, have been shared with researchers studying ocean currents, and their data has been used to argue for stricter international rules on fishing equipment. In this way, a very small community has contributed to a much larger debate.

[F] Visitors to the island are now asked to join a short beach clean during their stay, and many hotels offer a small discount to guests who take part. The council admits that the scheme is partly about raising awareness rather than removing large amounts of rubbish. Even so, several visitors have written to their own local councils after returning home, asking them to support the same international rules that Morra has campaigned for.

passages.title: Gardens that help wild bees
passages.text:
[A] Honeybees are well known, but they are only one of hundreds of bee species. Most wild bees live alone rather than in hives, and many are struggling because the flowers they depend on have disappeared from farmland and towns. In my opinion, private gardens could make a far bigger difference to these insects than most people realise.

[B] Together, gardens cover a surprisingly large area. In some suburbs, they make up a quarter of all the land. If even a small proportion of gardeners planted a variety of flowers that bloom from early spring to late autumn, wild bees would have food for much more of the year. Lawns that are cut less often also help, because small flowers such as clover are allowed to grow.

[C] It is a mistake, I believe, to think that only rare or expensive plants are useful. Many common herbs, including thyme and rosemary, are excellent sources of food for bees. What matters more is the shape of the flower: open, simple flowers are easier for bees to reach than the large, complex flowers often sold in garden centres.

[D] Garden chemicals are a more difficult issue. Some products used to kill insects that damage plants can also harm bees. Several countries have restricted certain chemicals, although scientists continue to debate how much harm each one causes. Until the evidence is clearer, gardeners would be wise to use as few chemicals as possible.

[E] Some towns have begun competitions for the most bee-friendly garden, and local schools have planted flower strips in their playgrounds. These efforts are small, but they show that helping wild bees does not require large farms or nature reserves – only a little space and some thought about what to plant.

[F] Gardeners who want to do more can also provide places for bees to nest. Many wild species lay their eggs in small holes in dead wood or in patches of bare, sunny soil, both of which are often removed in very tidy gardens. Leaving a corner of the garden a little untidy may therefore be one of the simplest and cheapest ways to help, although it may take some time for bees to find and use these new nesting sites.

A single large wildlife reserve outside the city

distractors.Planting only native flowers in every ne: Not chosen: the author discusses accessible ordinary gardens; an exclusively native planting requirement is more restrictive.
